updates.name: AISI 1018 Carbon Steel
updates.microstructure: Hypoeutectoid ferritic–pearlitic. Annealed: equiaxed proeutectoid ferrite (light, ~78–82 vol%) with pearlite colonies (dark lamellar Fe + Fe₃C, ~18–22% by lever rule at 0.18% C). Hot-rolled: similar phase fractions with finer pearlite spacing and some banding from solidification segregation. Cold-drawn bar: ferrite grains elongated along the drawing direction with banded pearlite stringers; deformation substructure raises hardness without phase change. Reveal with 2% nital (10–30 s); pearlite darkens, ferrite stays bright.
updates.heat_treatment: Anneal 870 °C / furnace cool; normalize 900 °C / air cool; carburize 900–950 °C for case hardening.

hardness_conditions.note: Surface depends on case depth (typ. 0.5–1.5 mm) and quench medium; core retains base ferritic–pearlitic structure.

updates.preparation_notes: Low-carbon ferritic–pearlitic steel. Prep aims to resolve pearlite lamellae without smearing the soft ferrite phase. Cold-drawn bar can show deformation artifacts (smearing, ferrite flow) if grinding pressure is too high. Use sharp SiC papers and minimize coarse-grit dwell time. Picral resolves pearlite lamellae better than nital when fine spacing matters; nital remains the day-to-day general-purpose etchant.

updates.name: AISI 1020 Carbon Steel
updates.microstructure: Hypoeutectoid ferritic–pearlitic, slightly higher pearlite fraction than 1018 (~22–26% pearlite by lever rule at 0.20% C). Annealed: equiaxed ferrite grains with pearlite colonies at boundaries. Hot-rolled bar: similar but with finer pearlite and occasional banding. The lower Mn (0.30–0.60 vs. 1018's 0.60–0.90) gives slightly larger ferrite grains and a more "open" structure under the microscope. Reveal with 2% nital; pearlite appears dark, ferrite white.
updates.heat_treatment: Anneal 870 °C / furnace cool; normalize 900 °C / air cool; carburize 900–925 °C for case hardening.

hardness_conditions.note: Common carburizing grade; surface depends on case depth and quench.

updates.preparation_notes: Standard low-carbon prep. Slightly softer than 1018 in equivalent supply condition. Same caveats: avoid heavy grinding pressure that smears ferrite; use picral if pearlite lamellae need to be resolved clearly.

updates.name: AISI 1035 Carbon Steel
updates.microstructure: Hypoeutectoid medium-carbon. Annealed: ~58–62% proeutectoid ferrite with ~38–42% pearlite colonies (lever rule at 0.35% C). Pearlite is the dominant strengthening constituent. Normalized: finer pearlite, slightly higher ferrite refinement. Quench-and-tempered: tempered martensite with possible retained ferrite if hardenability limits exceeded for the section. Reveal with 2% nital; use picral for pearlite lamellae spacing measurements or after Q&T.
updates.heat_treatment: Anneal 830 °C / furnace cool; normalize 870–900 °C / air cool; through-harden by water or oil quench from 830 °C and temper 200–650 °C.

hardness_conditions.note: Limited hardenability; suitable for thin sections only. For thicker sections expect mixed structure.

updates.preparation_notes: Medium-carbon prep. Pearlite fraction is high enough that resolution of the lamellar spacing is metallographically interesting — picral is recommended for that work. Q&T sections need a longer final polish (1 μm + 0.05 μm colloidal silica) to remove smearing and reveal tempered-martensite needle structure.

updates.name: AISI 1045 Carbon Steel
updates.microstructure: Near-eutectoid in pearlite content. Annealed/normalized: ~50–55% pearlite + ~45–50% proeutectoid ferrite at 0.45% C. Pearlite forms continuous network through ferrite. Quenched: martensite (typically lath/plate mixed) with possible retained ferrite or bainite in slow-cooled regions of larger sections — hardenability is limited without alloying. Q&T: tempered martensite, structure depends on temper temperature (carbide precipitation 200–300 °C, coarsening 400–650 °C). Reveal with 2% nital; picral for pearlite spacing.
updates.heat_treatment: Anneal 830 °C / furnace cool; normalize 870–900 °C / air cool; through-harden by water or oil quench from 830 °C; temper 200–650 °C per required strength.

hardness_conditions.note: Surface hardness on thin sections; through-hardening drops rapidly with section size due to limited hardenability.

updates.preparation_notes: Wide property range depending on heat treatment — always note the supplied condition before interpreting structure. Quenched 1045 can show mixed martensite-bainite-ferrite in larger sections because hardenability is marginal; this is a common case-study material for hardenability microscopy. For Q&T material, finish with 0.05 μm colloidal silica and a short Vilella etch to bring out tempered-martensite acicular features.

updates.name: AISI 1095 High Carbon Steel
updates.microstructure: Near-eutectoid (~0.95% C, eutectoid composition is 0.77%). Annealed (full anneal at 790 °C): coarse lamellar pearlite with a small amount of proeutectoid cementite at prior austenite grain boundaries. Spheroidized (subcritical anneal at ~700 °C, prolonged hold): globular Fe₃C in a ferrite matrix — the preferred condition for machining and metallographic baseline. Normalized: fine pearlite, prior-austenite grain boundaries decorated with thin cementite films. Quenched (water or oil from 790–820 °C): plate martensite (acicular) with retained austenite (up to ~5–10% depending on quench) and some retained cementite particles. Tempered (200–350 °C): tempered plate martensite, ε-carbide precipitation. Reveal with 2% nital for general structure, 4% picral for pearlite spacing and cementite networks.
updates.heat_treatment: Full anneal 790 °C / slow furnace cool; spheroidize at 700 °C for 6–12 h; harden by quench from 790–820 °C (water or oil) and temper 150–425 °C per intended use.

hardness_conditions.note: Brittle; not usable without tempering. Used in blade applications after 150–220 °C low temper.
Standard spring temper for music wire and flat springs.

updates.preparation_notes: High-carbon prep is sensitive. Spheroidized condition shows globular cementite — easy to confuse for poor polishing if you don't expect it. Quenched plate martensite is brittle and prone to edge chipping during sectioning and grinding; use a low-feed, well-cooled cutoff and mount with edge-retaining epoxy. Retained austenite is etched lighter than martensite by nital; quantify with picral + lever rule from BSE images if accurate phase fractions are needed.

updates.name: A36 Structural Steel
updates.composition: Fe-bal, ≤0.25–0.29 C (varies with thickness), 0.80–1.20 Mn (thicknesses >20 mm), ≤0.040 P, ≤0.050 S, ≤0.40 Si, 0.20 min Cu (when Cu specified) (ASTM A36/A36M)
updates.microstructure: Hypoeutectoid ferritic–pearlitic, similar to AISI 1020 but with deliberately higher Mn (and sometimes Si and Cu) for weldability and modest strengthening. As-rolled: equiaxed ferrite with banded pearlite — banding is often visible from slow cooling through the austenite-to-ferrite range during mill rolling. Pearlite fraction roughly 25–35% depending on C content within the spec window. Reveal with 2% nital. Banding is often the metallographically interesting feature on A36 sections (ASM HB v9, p.169).
updates.corrosion_resistance: low (atmospheric corrosion via standard rusting; not weathering steel)
updates.heat_treatment: Typically supplied as-rolled. Not specified for heat treatment in A36/A36M — if higher properties are required, switch to a higher-grade plate spec.

hardness_conditions.note: ASTM A36 does not specify hardness; values are typical from production. Thicker sections trend lower (slower cool).

strength_conditions.note: Elongation specified as ≥20% in 200 mm or ≥23% in 50 mm.

updates.preparation_notes: Standard structural steel prep. The banded ferrite–pearlite microstructure is the signature feature — don't over-polish, or banding contrast is reduced. Klemm I tinting can give nice color contrast between bands for QC photo-documentation. Avoid mixing samples from different thicknesses in the same montage — grain size and banding vary significantly with section.
